## Fuel conditions before and after precommercial thinning {#rt03-fuel-results}

```{r}
#| label: rt03-fuel-narrative-values
#| include: false
fuel_results <- read.csv(
  "outputs/fuel/tables/rd04-fuel-model-estimates.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
fuel_components <- c(
  one = "1-hour fuel",
  ten = "10-hour fuel",
  hundred = "100-hour fuel",
  coarse = "1,000-hour fuel",
  woody = "Woody vegetation",
  herb = "Herbaceous vegetation",
  litter = "Litter (pre-PCT only)",
  duff = "Duff (pre-PCT only)",
  reduction = "Woody vegetation difference (pre-PCT minus post-PCT)"
)
fuel_phases <- c(
  pre = "Pre-PCT",
  post = "Post-PCT",
  change = "Vegetation difference"
)
fuel_value <- function(
  component,
  phase,
  treatment,
  interval = FALSE,
  digits = 1L
) {
  cell <- fuel_results[
    fuel_results$component == fuel_components[[component]] &
      fuel_results$phase == fuel_phases[[phase]] &
      fuel_results$treatment == treatment,
  ]
  stopifnot(nrow(cell) == 1L)
  value <- formatC(cell$estimate, format = "f", digits = digits)
  if (interval) {
    value <- paste0(
      value,
      " (95% CI ",
      formatC(cell$lcl, format = "f", digits = digits),
      " to ",
      formatC(cell$ucl, format = "f", digits = digits),
      ")"
    )
  }
  value
}
```

### Dead fuel loading

Fuel measurements ten years after harvest characterized conditions before and
after precommercial thinning (PCT) across the four retention treatments
(@fig-rd04-fuel-inventory-manuscript). Following PCT, group selection
(GS) and low-density dispersed retention (LD) showed the largest estimated
increases in fine dead-fuel loads and reductions in woody standing vegetation.
These treatments also had the highest post-PCT fine dead-fuel loads. Pre-PCT
dead-fuel estimates suggested subtler, component-specific treatment patterns.
Fuel loads are reported as
model-estimated means, with 95% confidence intervals. Woody and herbaceous
standing vegetation are reported separately, as are pre-PCT litter and duff. All
loads and load differences below are in Mg ha^-1^.

Before PCT, estimated 1-hour fuel loads were highest in high-density
aggregated retention (HA;
`r fuel_value("one", "pre", "ha")`) and lowest in GS
(`r fuel_value("one", "pre", "gs")`), with LD and
high-density dispersed (HD) retention intermediate. Estimated 10-hour loads
ranged from `r fuel_value("ten", "pre", "hd")` in HD to
`r fuel_value("ten", "pre", "gs")` in GS, and 100-hour loads from
`r fuel_value("hundred", "pre", "hd")` to
`r fuel_value("hundred", "pre", "gs")` in those same treatments.
The 1,000-hour class had larger mean loads, ranging from
`r fuel_value("coarse", "pre", "ld")` in LD to
`r fuel_value("coarse", "pre", "gs", interval = TRUE)` in GS.
Uncertainty was substantial for this coarse-wood component across treatments.

The separated forest-floor components showed different treatment patterns.
Pre-PCT litter estimates ranged from `r fuel_value("litter", "pre", "ld")`
in LD to `r fuel_value("litter", "pre", "gs")` in GS; HA and HD were
intermediate. Duff estimates were lowest in HA, at
`r fuel_value("duff", "pre", "ha", interval = TRUE)`, and highest in HD, at
`r fuel_value("duff", "pre", "hd", interval = TRUE)`, with GS and LD
both near 28–29. These are model-derived forest-floor loads based on the
estimated litter-depth boundary. Post-PCT litter and duff were not estimated
because the forest-floor boundary could not be distinguished reliably in the
presence of slash and suspended foliage.

After PCT, estimated 1-hour loads were about 2.4–2.7 in GS, LD, and HD,
and `r fuel_value("one", "post", "ha")` in HA. The 10-hour estimates were
ordered GS (`r fuel_value("ten", "post", "gs")`), LD
(`r fuel_value("ten", "post", "ld")`), HA
(`r fuel_value("ten", "post", "ha")`), and HD
(`r fuel_value("ten", "post", "hd")`). The 100-hour estimates followed the
same order, from `r fuel_value("hundred", "post", "gs", interval = TRUE)`
in GS to `r fuel_value("hundred", "post", "hd", interval = TRUE)` in HD.
Post-PCT 1,000-hour means ranged from `r fuel_value("coarse", "post", "ha")`
in HA to `r fuel_value("coarse", "post", "gs")` in GS, with wide confidence
intervals. These rankings describe estimated loads; they do not establish
pairwise treatment differences. The separate dead-fuel phase estimates are
reference conditions, without paired phase-change tests in this display.

### Standing vegetation and woody vegetation difference

Pre-PCT woody standing-vegetation means were greatest in GS
(`r fuel_value("woody", "pre", "gs")`), followed by LD
(`r fuel_value("woody", "pre", "ld")`), HD
(`r fuel_value("woody", "pre", "hd")`), and HA
(`r fuel_value("woody", "pre", "ha")`). Post-PCT means were 2.0–2.9 across
treatments. The joint phase model estimated pre-minus-post reductions
of `r fuel_value("reduction", "change", "gs", interval = TRUE)` in GS,
`r fuel_value("reduction", "change", "ld", interval = TRUE)` in LD,
`r fuel_value("reduction", "change", "ha", interval = TRUE)` in HA, and
`r fuel_value("reduction", "change", "hd", interval = TRUE)` in HD.
All four reduction intervals excluded zero. Their uncertainty includes the
pre/post covariance; the ordering of reduction estimates alone does not test
differences among treatments.

Herbaceous standing-vegetation means were small relative to woody loads:
0.24–0.59 before PCT and 0.11–0.35 afterward, with broad relative uncertainty.
The woody reduction represents an inferred potential contribution to surface
fuels. It does not measure slash deposition or reconcile standing-vegetation
loss with changes in downed fuel classes. Without a contemporaneous unthinned
comparison, the phase transition does not isolate a causal PCT effect.
